text: The purchaser will likely prevail because his predecessor (the woman) held an easement that was properly recorded and subsequently merged into the man's title when he acquired both properties; however, upon selling to the third-party purchaser without reserving or conveying the right-of-way in their deed, the original burden on the land remained with the seller-man while the benefit attached to the purchased house. Since the merger doctrine does not automatically extinguish an easement if it is later severed by a sale of one parcel over another, and because the man's subsequent attempt to block access violates the purchaser's implied or retained rights derived from the original recorded instrument, the court will enforce the existing easement against the landowner who created it. CONFIDENCE: 85
